core_idea: Track only the position of the least significant set bit of each pile. The minimum such position determines the outcome: an odd minimum lets the first player move to a losing state, an even minimum with all values equal gives the second player a win, and an even minimum with unequal values allows both players to avoid termination indefinitely, producing a draw.
key_observations: A pile is playable exactly when its least significant set-bit position is positive; the game ends when all such positions are zero.
If every pile has the same least significant set-bit position c, choosing any pile changes every pile's position to c - 1.
If m is the minimum least significant set-bit position, choosing a pile attaining m makes every pile's position equal to m - 1.
When m is odd, the first move reaches a state with an even common position, which is losing for the next player.
When m is even and every pile has position m, every move reaches a state with an odd common position, so the current player loses under optimal play.

When m is even and some piles have position m while others have a larger position, a player can repeatedly choose a pile with position greater than m, preserving both types of piles and preventing the terminal state.
Configurations can be counted by the exact minimum position using a difference of counts for lower-bound conditions.
The second-player winning configurations require all piles to have the same even least significant set-bit position.
reasoning_patterns: Replace large numeric states with the smallest structural feature that controls legal moves and transitions.
Identify a synchronized state in which one operation transforms every component in the same way.
Classify positions by a decisive minimum and by whether all components attain that minimum.
Use parity of a decreasing measure to determine which player receives a losing position.
Prove a draw by exhibiting a strategy that preserves an invariant indefinitely rather than trying to analyze all future states.
Count objects with an exact minimum by subtracting configurations satisfying successive lower-bound conditions.
Separate outcome cases structurally before performing combinatorial counting.
questions: What minimal feature of each component determines whether a move is possible?
Can the full state be compressed to a small summary such as a minimum, parity, or rank?
What happens when all components share the same critical value?
Can one move synchronize or normalize all components?
What does fixing the minimum imply about the next state?
Does the parity of a monotone quantity determine who receives a losing position?
Can either player preserve a nonterminal invariant forever?
Can exact-minimum cases be counted as a difference of lower-bound cases?
Which outcome cases require equality across all components, rather than only a minimum?
